vignette:
Jamal, a 59-year-old professor, sat at his desk, staring blankly at the papers strewn around him. The once-vibrant energy he had for teaching and research had been replaced by a heaviness that clung to him, a consequence of the traumatic event that had forever altered his life. It was two years ago when he received the devastating news: his younger brother, who had been battling chronic illness, had drowned during an unexpected flood that swept through their hometown. The sheer horror of that moment replayed in his mind, the anguished cries of his family, and the images of the murky water engulfing his brother, haunting him relentlessly. Now, even the sight of water—whether it be a calm lake, a flowing river, or even a mere puddle—sent his heart racing and his body into a state of panic that he could not control. Each encounter with these triggers ignited a feeling of danger that felt all too real, as if his body was warning him that loss could happen again at any moment. The sight of water transformed into a cue that sent his heart racing, leading him to feel a visceral sense of threat, as if the very essence of danger was woven into those moments, echoing the trauma he had endured. Each time these reminders emerged, they ignited an immediate sense of danger that felt all too real, leading him to believe that loss was lurking just beneath the surface, ready to strike again. Each encounter with these triggers led to an overwhelming sense of danger, as if the threat of loss loomed just as it had on that fateful day, flooding his mind with vivid memories that he could not escape. Each encounter with these triggers deepened his sense of danger, a visceral reminder that his world was still fraught with the threat of loss, amplifying the fear that he could not escape the memory of that day. 

Jamal's body had learned to react to danger instinctively, often before he could even register what was happening. Each time he encountered the triggering sights or smells associated with that fateful day, he felt his pulse quicken, his hands tremble, and a sense of dread wash over him. The constant background hum of threat made even the most mundane cues feel charged with warning, confirming his belief that he was perpetually in danger of reliving his trauma. This pervasive sense of threat shaped his perception, causing him to view ordinary moments as potential triggers, each one amplifying the anxiety that coursed through him. With the constant background hum of danger, Jamal found that even benign stimuli could morph into reminders of loss, each sight or sound reinforcing his belief that danger was ever-present, just waiting to resurface. Living at that pitch of alertness, Jamal found that almost anything could tip into a warning, as the constant hum of danger made even innocuous sights resonate with the fear of reliving that day. Living with this persistent sense of threat, Jamal found that ordinary sounds and sights would suddenly trigger memories of his brother's drowning, each new reminder reinforcing his anxiety and fear. His students often brought bottled water into the classroom, the sound of the bottles crinkling would send shivers up his spine, as the faint scent of musty dampness would fill the air. He had begun to dread these moments, each triggering experience reinforcing his fear that he was still trapped in that day of loss, unable to move forward. The more he tried to rationalize these feelings, the more they spiraled, leaving him feeling helpless. 

Despite his academic achievements, Jamal struggled with overwhelming negative emotions that accompanied his memories. Guilt gnawed at him for not being there to save his brother, and anger bubbled beneath the surface at the unfairness of it all. Even in the safety of his own home, he found it impossible to relax, constantly on high alert for the next reminder of his loss. His inability to find peace seeped into every aspect of his life, affecting his ability to teach and connect with his students. He had retreated from social gatherings, avoiding family events where the presence of water was likely, and isolating himself from friends who wanted to help but did not understand the depth of his pain. 

Jamal felt trapped in a cycle that tightened around him with each passing day. The more he avoided triggers, the more his world shrank, and the more he felt his body react to perceived dangers, reinforcing his belief that he was perpetually under threat. Each day became a battle against the flood of memories and feelings that seized him without warning, leaving him feeling exhausted and defeated. He often tried to distract himself with work or movies, but the stress of his avoidance weighed heavily on him, and his body continued to betray him with physical reactions that he could not control. 

Finally, after months of internal struggle, Jamal came to a breaking point. He realized that he could not continue down this path alone. The isolation had become unbearable, and he feared that his passion for teaching would be extinguished forever if he did not seek help. What frightened him most was the thought of never being able to escape the shadows of his trauma, of living in a constant state of anxiety and dread. As he sat alone in his office, he made the decision to reach out for professional support, hoping that maybe, just maybe, he could find a way to navigate through the pain and reclaim his life.
